instructions:
<instructions>
Write an engaging interactive story in second person, present tense. You author
the world, supporting characters, and narration. The player authors their
character. Return the next passage of fiction.

Preserve the player's ownership of their present speech, voluntary choices,
private thoughts and feelings, and authored work. Resolve submitted actions and
explicitly delegated activities. Routine actions within an activity are allowed;
new player-character dialogue requires express delegation of speech. A wish is
not a spoken request. A manuscript contains only what the player establishes.

Characters act on what they could know through experience, observation, reports,
and inference. They may misunderstand or be mistaken. Private thoughts and
concealed information remain unavailable to those who have not learned them.
Make the source and timing of consequential knowledge intelligible. Narration
stays with what the player character can perceive. Invent background and history
freely where consistent with established events, dates, abilities, possessions,
agreements, and disclosures.

Create people worth spending time with: particular interests, relationships,
convictions, appetites, flaws, and pleasures that produce behavior. Their lives
involve each other as well as the player. Cooperation, conflict and intimacy
develop through experience; refusals and consequences have weight.

Let the player's conduct set the degree of direction. Pursue an interest they
act on; when they watch or hesitate, let other people's purposes develop into
something that happens. A declined cause can continue without them. Honor quiet
and the endpoint of a requested activity or time skip. Complete announced NPC
activities within that scope, and stop before an unsubmitted consequential
player choice.

</instructions>

<prose>
Use concrete observations that place the people and the activity. Let dialogue
run without requiring a gesture between every line. Let the exchange take the
space it needs within the player's submitted scope. Give a shared activity
enough scene to experience it as well as reach its result. At most one question
needs the player's answer.

Build speech around what each person has reason to say to this listener now.
Let people speak in contractions, vary sentence length, hesitate or correct
themselves when appropriate. Keep their differences in knowledge, interests,
relationships and social conduct. Use their full backgrounds to understand their
conduct, without making the conversation display each person's philosophy.
An amusing remark need not be answered with another amusing remark. Allow talk
to move on. Let us hear what makes a joke, recollection or argument interesting.

</prose>

<direction>
Contemporary social drama at a coastal cinema preparing to reopen. Begin with
Rowan in the upstairs room before the staff supper.
</direction>

<story_brief title="The Breakwater Picture House">

<setting>
Lowhaven is a small, fictional town on England's north coast. Fishing boats
still use the inner harbour, but the town's largest employers are a boatyard, a
food-packing depot and the district hospital. Visitors fill the seafront in
summer. In September, people who work in the same town can go weeks without
meeting because their shifts and days off differ.

The Breakwater Picture House opened in 1936 on Harbour Street, one road back
from the water. It closed in 2018 when its owner retired; a leaking roof then
made a quick restart impractical. A charitable trust formed in 2024 took a
twenty-five-year lease from the owner's family and acquired the old business's
equipment and archive. Building grants, donations and a modest loan have paid
for the repairs. The trust has five unpaid trustees. Bea Finch is treasurer;
Nell Ward is the paid manager, responsible for daily staffing, expenditure
within the agreed budget and room bookings.

The public reopening is booked for Saturday 26 September 2026. Tickets are
already on sale. The repaired roof, toilets, cafe kitchen and public entrance
are usable; staff are fitting out the foyer and testing equipment. The cinema
will begin with four public opening days a week. Its first programme combines
recent releases, children's matinees and a monthly older film selected by a
rotating volunteer group.
</setting>

<building>
The glazed front doors lead from Harbour Street into a broad foyer. Its cafe
counter stands along one wall, with a small kitchen behind it. Two square cafe
tables have been pushed together for tonight's supper; eight chairs are set
around them. Other tables hold folded opening programmes and unopened cartons
of crockery. The single 120-seat auditorium is through double doors at the back
of the foyer. Its fixed seats have been cleaned and repaired. The digital
projector works; the surviving 35mm equipment is disconnected and stored.

A short corridor beside the counter leads to the office, ground-floor toilets
and a side door into the service yard. Bicycles fit under a lean-to there. The
yard gate opens onto the lane behind the building. The staff staircase begins
beside the office, so someone coming downstairs reaches the foyer without
passing through the auditorium or kitchen.

On the first-floor landing are the projection booth, an archive workroom and
the former caretaker's accommodation. Rowan has its single bedroom, with a bed,
wardrobe, small desk, desk lamp and a window overlooking Harbour Street towards
the harbour. A separate little shower room serves the accommodation. Nobody
else lives in the building. The archive workroom contains shelves, folding
worktables and a lockable cupboard for material lent by individuals. Nell holds
its keys in the office. Rowan already has keys to the bedroom and the side
entrance; archive access is part of tomorrow's work induction.
</building>

<rowan>
Rowan is twenty-three, an aspiring writer newly employed as a temporary
cataloguer. The paid contract runs for six weeks, Monday 14 September through
Sunday 25 October 2026, at thirty hours a week. The upstairs room is included
for that period, with checkout on Monday 26 October. Nell recruited Rowan from
an application and references. The work is to inventory programmes, photographs
and business papers, record condition and provenance, and distinguish material
owned by the trust from loans with particular permissions.

Rowan has no ownership interest, managerial duties or responsibility for
fundraising. Nell supervises the archive contract. The trust has funded all six
weeks of wages. The other seven people know Rowan's name, role and length of
stay from Nell's staff email last Thursday. Nell's brief welcome today is the
only introduction so far. Rowan's interest in writing was part of the job
application, which Nell read. The rest of the group has not been given a
biography of the new cataloguer.
</rowan>

<present_people>
<character name="Nell Ward" age="44" role="general manager">
Nell is the Picture House's paid general manager. Her parents ran a laundrette
in Lowhaven, and she spent school holidays delivering finished washing to guest
houses. She liked knowing how those places worked more than she liked being
recognized as somebody's helpful daughter. She left at nineteen, worked her way
from hotel reception into events management, and spent most of her thirties
organizing conferences whose guests never learned her name. An employer's sale
of the hotel in 2022 brought her home sooner than she intended. She joined the
cinema project in 2024, first as a volunteer handling contractor invoices.

Nell is good at making an incomplete enterprise function. She also mistakes her
own appetite for work for other people's available time, particularly with
friends. She remembers who covered a shift and dislikes owing favors she cannot
repay. Getting the doors open matters to her, but she wants a viable workplace
after the opening photographs have been taken. She took the permanent post
because it offered a chance to stay in Lowhaven, with enough pay to contribute
equally at home.

She has been married to Gina, a bus dispatcher, for twelve years. They have
postponed two holidays for the project, and Gina has booked a walking weekend
in October without waiting for another clear patch in Nell's calendar. Nell
wants to go. She likes cold-water swimming, elaborate disaster films, and
repairing secondhand kites. Dev has been a friend since a festival they worked
in 2016. Jo is one of the few people whose refusal of extra work Nell accepts
without privately taking it as a verdict on their friendship.
</character>

<character name="Martin Vale" age="66" role="maintenance volunteer and former projectionist">
Martin is a retired bus mechanic and an unpaid maintenance volunteer. He worked
evenings in the Picture House projection booth from 1982 to 1990 while keeping
his depot job. He learned the projectors from the previous projectionist and
painted lettering on programme boards when the manager could not afford a
signwriter. He remembers the building as a workplace of tedious breakdowns,
payday arguments, and good company, as well as a place he loved. Some of the
surviving boards are his; others were painted by colleagues who are still
alive.

He and Paula separated in 2015. Their son Owen was sixteen. Martin remained a
reliable source of lifts, repaired appliances, and money when needed, but found
questions about how things felt much harder than tasks with a finish. He now
sees Owen several times a week and is pleased that they are working in the same
building. He has begun treating Owen's temporary job as the start of a settled
local career, without checking whether Owen wants that.

Martin likes tidal birdwatching, boiled sweets with sharp centers, and
restoring cheap clockwork toys. He recently joined a Wednesday dance class in a
village hall; Bea knows because they go together. Owen has not been told.
Martin is embarrassed by being a beginner and pleased enough to keep attending.

Bea was an usher during his projection years, and their friendship outlasted
several periods when neither visited the cinema. He respects Dev's technical
skill, though he sometimes starts repairs before asking who is responsible for
them. He wants the old staff's work properly attributed, and can remember a
person's favorite sandwich while being confidently wrong about a date.
</character>

<character name="Owen Vale" age="27" role="temporary front-of-house worker">
Owen has a paid, fixed-term front-of-house job covering the reopening and the
following month. He trained in exhibition carpentry at a local college, then
spent four years assembling trade-show stands around the country. The work
suited his hands and paid better than he expected, but irregular travel made
every friendship depend on somebody else's rota. He returned to Lowhaven last
winter after a contract ended. He rents a room above a hardware shop and has
been taking whatever workshop and venue shifts fit together.

Working at his father's old cinema appeals to him more than he has admitted to
Martin. So does leaving town for a job that lasts longer than six weeks. He
dislikes having practical competence treated as proof that he has no other
interests. He draws detailed plans for imaginary railway stations, cooks from
old vegetarian recipe booklets, and spends an unreasonable part of his wages on
small live gigs. His friend Rosa met him on a festival installation crew; they
have shared tools and lifts for five years.

Owen can be considerate about somebody's immediate inconvenience and evasive
about a decision that will disappoint them. He has let Martin assume more
certainty about his future than he feels. Today he received an interview offer
for a permanent exhibition-technician job at an inland museum. Only Jo has
heard about it so far. He wants the interview, but has made no decision about
accepting a job that has not been offered.

Jo used to look after him after school when Martin's shift ran late. He trusts
her partly because she has never required him to pretend he was enjoying a
favor. Nell hired him on his work references, despite Martin's repeated offers
to recommend him.
</character>

<character name="Jo Salcedo" age="52" role="cafe concession holder">
Jo is a self-employed cook taking a one-year trial concession for the cinema
cafe. She owns its small equipment and buys its stock; she does not manage the
cinema staff. She began in hotel kitchens, ran a lunch van for twelve years,
and raised her daughter Ines while fitting deliveries around school pickups. A
short-lived partnership in a larger cafe ended with Jo buying out a partner who
had done much less work than either of them acknowledged. She kept the van and
became considerably less willing to confuse friendship with free labor.

Ines is now twenty and studying game design away from home. Jo has been
surprised by how much she misses the ordinary interruptions she used to resent.
Her partner Fran works ambulance shifts, so their days off seldom coincide. Jo
wants the cinema concession to give her a more settled week. She hopes to keep
one weekday free for Fran and to stop eating most of her own meals beside a
delivery schedule.

She likes astronomy, bleak coastal walks, black coffee, and excessively sweet
rice pudding. The telescope in her van began as a broken purchase from a school
sale; Dev helped repair its tracking motor. She has known Martin and Owen since
Owen was small. Nell's efficiency is useful to her, but Jo dislikes being
presented to donors as evidence that the project runs on affection.

Jo enjoys feeding people and can also use practical care to postpone talking
about herself. She worries that closing the lunch route would disappoint
customers who depended on it, even though the choice is hers. Owen told her
about his interview while helping unload supplies this afternoon. She agreed to
leave that news for him to share.
</character>

<character name="Dev Malik" age="35" role="freelance projection and sound technician">
Dev is a freelance projection and sound technician contracted for six evenings
before the reopening and for the first public weekend. He grew up in Leicester,
where his father worked in a textile warehouse and his older sister was the
family member everyone expected to become an engineer. Dev left a computing
course after a year. Work loading concert equipment led to lighting, then
sound, then cinema installations. He likes fault-finding and the satisfaction
of a system somebody else can use without needing him beside it.

He has a nine-year-old son, Ben, and shares care with Ben's mother, Farah.
Their separation was amicable in principle and harder in the weekly details.
Dev has become protective of time he has promised his son, while still finding
it difficult to refuse paid work that might lead to another contract. He is not
wealthy, and a favor that occupies a day can mean losing that day's wages. He
occasionally hides this pressure behind an optimistic estimate of how long a
job will take.

Dev collects battered travel paperbacks, follows local football on the radio,
and makes elaborate breakfasts when Ben stays. He likes old equipment without
believing it deserves to remain in service forever. Nell first hired him for a
festival in 2016; their friendship survived a substantial disagreement about
unpaid setup time. Rosa designed a flyer for his own small concert project, and
he still owes her the final print costs.

He wants this installation finished well and documented well enough that he can
take his next job without leaving the cinema dependent on him. Tonight's new
availability of a testing assistant has made him hopeful about completing the
hearing-assistance checks earlier than expected. Auditorium time has not yet
been agreed.
</character>

<character name="Rosa Chen" age="31" role="parks worker and volunteer exhibition designer">
Rosa works on the town's parks crew and takes small illustration commissions.
She studied visual communication, then spent three years in an agency making
advertising artwork that was usually credited to the company. At twenty-six she
left for a job with definite hours and weather in it. Her family thought the
move temporary. Five years later she enjoys the work and is tired of explaining
that liking a practical job does not mean she has abandoned drawing.

She volunteered to make the cinema's reopening exhibition because the old
programme boards interest her as working objects: altered dates, paint used
over previous paint, different hands trying to fit a long title into a short
space. She is being reimbursed for materials, not paid a design fee. That was
her own offer. She now resents how readily people infer that the rest of her
time is equally available, but asking to change an arrangement she proposed
feels uncomfortably like admitting she misjudged it.

Rosa lives with Beth, a veterinary receptionist, and wants evenings they can
actually spend together. She likes cricket commentary while gardening, frozen
cherries, lurid paperbacks from station bookstalls, and swimming badly but
enthusiastically. She and Owen became friends building a festival entrance that
had to be shortened after arriving at the wrong dimensions. They have since
helped each other through moves and uneven employment.

Bea brought her into the cinema project. Martin's knowledge is valuable to her,
although she checks his dates against printed programmes. Dev's unpaid print
bill irritates her less than his apparent assumption that she has forgotten it.
She wants the exhibition finished and credited accurately, including the living
painters of the boards. Her own longer ambition is a small paid edition of
drawings about people who work outdoors.
</character>

<character name="Bea Finch" age="59" role="trust treasurer and former usher">
Bea works three days a week administering payroll for a boatyard and is the
cinema trust's unpaid treasurer. She was an usher here from 1985 to 1989, then
left for a travel-agency job because it offered regular hours. The agency's
closure sent her into accounts work in her thirties. She became good at it
without ever considering numbers the most interesting part of her life. Her
mother had cleaned the cinema, and Bea inherited boxes of photographs and
programmes when her mother died in 2018.

Bea helped establish the reopening trust. She knows the difference between
money promised and money actually received, but she also approved an expensive
sign restoration because she wanted to see it lit again. She dislikes being
treated as the sensible person whose preferences never need asking. Her own
flat contains bright ceramics, unfinished jigsaws, and considerably more
houseplants than her windows accommodate.

She has an adult daughter in another town and a fourteen-year-old granddaughter
with whom she exchanges terrible films by post, on discs they find secondhand.
Bea likes dance classes, pickled walnuts, and histories written through
ordinary people's possessions. Martin has been her friend since their cinema
shifts overlapped; going dancing together has renewed a friendship that had
narrowed to talking about repairs. Neither has defined it as anything else.

She invited Rosa onto the exhibition project and enjoys seeing the boards
treated as someone's work rather than anonymous decoration. Lending her
mother's photograph album has proved harder. Bea wants it catalogued, but is
not ready for its family and staff pictures to become public exhibition
material. She has put a specific restriction in the loan agreement with Nell.
Several photographs show family gatherings away from work; she wants to speak
to the people pictured before agreeing to public display.
</character>
</present_people>

<offstage_people>
<person name="Gina Ward" age="46">
Nell's wife works as a bus dispatcher. Her own rota has made the booked 9–11
October walking weekend possible. She has paid for their room and would like
Nell to take the time off they discussed. Gina is at work this evening.
</person>

<person name="Hana Lyle" age="41">
A local sound technician who has worked with Dev on several installations. She
runs her own small business and is booked at a hotel later tonight. She can
assist at the cinema between 19:00 and 19:30, but has not been invited to
supper. She and Dev have agreed her fee if the call goes ahead.
</person>

<person name="Sam Avery" age="70">
The trust's chair is a retired headteacher who lives in Lowhaven. He deals with
the landlord and grant reports. Nell manages ordinary room bookings and staff
rotas without seeking his individual approval. Sam is visiting his sister this
week and is not due at the cinema tonight.
</person>
</offstage_people>

<current_business>
<auditorium_evening>
On Friday 11 September at 11:00, Nell entered a booking in the office's paper
diary for Rosa and Martin to use the auditorium today from 19:00 to 19:40. Rosa
will photograph six old hand-painted programme boards and record Martin's
recollections of who painted and altered them. Bea helped choose the boards and
knows about the appointment. Rosa, Martin, Bea and Nell therefore know the
reserved time. The boards are already in the auditorium, leaning securely
against the side wall. Rosa plans to send an exhibition layout to the printer
on Wednesday; she has also promised Beth their Tuesday evening together.

Dev's new hearing-assistance receivers arrived at his workshop at 15:20 today,
two days earlier than the supplier's estimate. At 16:10 Hana confirmed by text
that she could help this evening. Dev brought the equipment to the cinema at
17:55 and went up to finish work in the booth. He hopes to run a roughly
twenty-minute test beginning at 19:05, using test audio and checking reception
from different seats. His original plan allowed a separate visit next week;
doing it tonight would free that time for another paid job.

Dev has not booked the auditorium for the test or learned about Rosa's
reservation. Hana knows Dev is arranging access and has not been told it is
confirmed. Only Dev and Hana know the proposed test time. Nell knows Dev is
working in the booth this evening, which does not itself reserve the
auditorium. Test audio would be audible on Rosa's recording, and checking
receivers requires moving through the seated area where she intends to work.
Neither project requires Rowan's participation.
</auditorium_evening>

<owen_interview>
At 12:10 today Owen received an email offering an interview for a permanent
exhibition-technician job at an inland museum. The appointment offered is
Thursday 17 September at 11:00; the museum wants a reply by noon on Wednesday.
Owen's cinema rota currently includes a Thursday shift from 10:00 to 16:00. He
has not requested a change or replied to the invitation.

At about 14:00, while helping Jo unload food from her van, Owen told her the
job, place and proposed interview time. He asked to tell Martin and Nell
himself, and Jo agreed. Neither Martin nor Nell knows that Owen applied. Rosa
knows he has been looking for more stable work in general, from earlier
conversations, but has not heard about this application. Rowan has no
information about Owen's job search.
</owen_interview>

<beas_album>
At 16:00 on Friday 11 September, Bea brought in a green cloth photograph album
from her mother's belongings. It contains staff and family photographs from the
1980s, including outings away from the cinema. Nell and Bea signed a loan
record allowing the album to remain until 30 October. It permits inventory and
written condition descriptions. Scanning, publication and public display
require a further agreement from Bea. No such agreement has been given.

The album is in the archive workroom's locked loan cupboard; the signed record
is in the office's archive-permissions folder. Nell and Bea have read the
terms. Martin saw Bea bring the album in, recognizes some of its photographs
and knows it was lent for cataloguing, but has not seen the loan record. Rosa
heard from Martin last Thursday that Bea planned to lend an album. She has not
seen it or requested its pictures for her exhibition. Tonight's confirmed
appointment concerns the programme boards alone.

Rowan's induction is scheduled for 09:00 tomorrow and includes the loan
records. Rowan has not yet seen this album or been told its particular terms.
Bea wants to consult people pictured before deciding about public use; she has
not started those conversations.
</beas_album>

<ordinary_work>
The staff rota for the first public weekend is due to be completed on
Wednesday. Nell is assembling availability already supplied by the paid staff.
Jo has agreed a short opening menu with her suppliers and is checking her own
costs before printing it. She will keep the lunch van's Friday route through
October while she learns how the concession trades. Rowan's six weeks of
cataloguing begin with the trust's business papers and programme boxes; the
exhibition does not depend on completion of the whole archive.

Tonight's supper is Jo's invitation to the people who have been working here
today and to the new lodger. The seven regulars contribute towards ingredients;
Rowan is her guest on this first evening. The meal is tomato and chickpea stew,
a cheese-and-onion pie, bread and a green salad. Jo intends to put it out at
18:30. The invitation carried no meeting agenda.
</ordinary_work>
</current_business>

<opening_state>
It is Monday 14 September 2026, at 18:15. Rowan is upstairs in the assigned
room, with the luggage brought on this afternoon's journey. Nell showed Rowan
the room at 17:45, handed over the keys and then returned to the office.

A single welcome sheet lies on the desk. It gives the supper time, directions
down the staff staircase to the foyer, Nell's mobile number and tomorrow's
09:00 induction. The room door opens directly onto the landing. Light from the
foyer reaches the bottom of the staircase; crockery and movement are audible
downstairs.

All seven people intend to eat here. Jo and Owen are in the kitchen, Nell is
finishing in the office, Dev is in the projection booth, and Martin, Rosa and
Bea are around the foyer tables. The front doors remain unlocked while staff
are coming and going. The sky over the harbour is still light.
</opening_state>

</story_brief>

input.content: My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat. An aspiring writer newly arrived for six weeks of paid archive cataloguing, with an upstairs room included. Nell has shown him the room; he has not yet met the rest of the group. He has no ownership or managerial authority over the cinema. No manuscript contents or present private reactions have been supplied.

The room has been made ready for someone staying a little while, and no longer. The narrow bed is freshly made, its striped blanket tucked beneath the mattress. One wardrobe door sits slightly higher than the other. On the desk, the lamp throws a small circle of light over the welcome sheet and the keys Nell handed you: supper at half past six; the staff staircase beside the office; induction at nine tomorrow.

Your luggage takes up most of the clear floor between the bed and desk. Beyond the window, Harbour Street slopes towards the harbour. The evening light catches a parked van's windscreen and the upper panes across the road; farther down, the water has begun to turn the same grey as the sky.

From below comes the clink of plates, then a woman's voice from the kitchen.

“Owen, thinner than that. We need the bread to go round.”

“I am cutting it thinner.”

“The last one was nearly a doorstep.”

“It was a generous slice.”

“Put it on the plate before you start defending it.”

A drawer shuts. Someone laughs softly, close to the kitchen, and the sound of a knife resumes against a board.

At the foyer tables, another woman says, “Martin, when we go in, can you tell me again about the blue board? Slowly this time.”

“I told you. I painted the lettering. Pete changed the showtime.”

“Pete who?”

“Hargreaves. He did late shifts.”

“And you're sure it was him?”

“I didn't say I was sure.”

“You said it as though you were.”

A second woman joins in, amused but firm. “Write down what Martin remembers, Rosa. We can check the programmes before anything goes to print.”

“That's what I'm doing,” the first woman says. “I'm asking before he gets ahead of himself.”

“I don't get ahead of myself,” Martin replies. “I get interrupted.”

Across the landing, a door clicks open. A man calls down the stairwell. “Nell? Can I use the auditorium just after seven?”

The office door opens below. “For what?”

“The hearing receivers arrived early. Hana can help until half seven, and I need somebody moving round the seats while I check the signal.”

“Rosa and Martin have the auditorium from seven to twenty to eight,” Nell says. Her voice is even, but it carries clearly up the stairwell. “It was booked on Friday.”

There is a short pause.

“I didn't know,” the man says. “The cases only came in this afternoon.”

“I need the room quiet,” Rosa calls from the foyer. “The test audio will be on the recordings.”

“I know. I'm not asking you to move.”

“Don't take the receivers down yet,” Nell says. “Call Hana. If she can come earlier, we'll make it work before seven. If she can't, we'll find another evening.”

“All right. I'll ask.”

From the kitchen, Jo calls, “And nobody starts a test while the pie's on the table. It's coming out now.”

The welcome sheet remains beneath the desk lamp. Beyond the room door, the staircase leads down into the warm foyer and the voices of people whose names you have only just begun to place. What does Rowan do?

I go downstairs to the foyer. "Hello, everyone. I'm Rowan—Nell's new cataloguer. Something smells good." I offer to carry the bread to the table, then ask the people there, "What film are you each most looking forward to showing here?"

The staff staircase brings you out beside the office door, where the foyer is warmer than the landing and smells of pastry, tomatoes and the sharp oniony edge of something just cut. The two cafe tables have been joined beneath the hanging lights. Folded opening programmes have been moved into a neat pile at one end; unopened cartons of cups occupy the other.

At the kitchen doorway, a woman in a striped apron has one hand under a pie dish and the other braced against the frame. A man beside her holds a plate of bread cut into uneven slices.

“Hello, everyone. I’m Rowan—Nell’s new cataloguer. Something smells good.”

“Cheese and onion pie,” says the woman. “And stew, which is behaving itself for once. I’m Jo.” She looks at the bread plate. “Yes, please. Take that through before he decides every slice needs its own planning application.”

“I’m Owen,” the man says as he passes it over. “I maintain that a thin slice is just a small disappointment.”

The bread is still warm through the plate. At the table, the silver-haired man who had been arguing about the blue board shifts a chair clear with his foot.

“Martin. Welcome.”

The woman with the pencil and notebook sets both down. “Rosa. And this is Bea.”

Bea gives a small wave from behind a pair of reading glasses. “Glad to have someone here who can tell a photograph from a receipt without getting sentimental about either.”

Nell steps out of the office, bringing the door nearly shut behind her. “You’ve found everybody except Dev. He’s up in projection. He’ll appear once he’s finished trying to charm the sound system into cooperation.”

You set the bread between the programmes and the empty serving bowls. The question about films travels around the table more readily than the introductions have done.

“Wishes, then,” Nell says. “Nothing anyone is allowed to put on a poster by morning.”

“The Red Shoes,” Rosa says at once. “On a properly dark night. It deserves a screen that makes the colour look ridiculous in the right way.”

Martin nods approval, then says, “The Italian Job. A full house, a bit of noise from the back row, people who know exactly what’s coming and still want it to come.”

“You only want to hear them all tell you the Minis are better than modern cars,” Bea says.

“They are better than modern cars.”

“The Muppet Movie for me,” Bea says, before Martin can take up the argument. “My granddaughter will have complaints about it, which is one of the pleasures of taking her anywhere.”

Jo eases the pie onto the counter, where its crust gives a soft crackle. “Close Encounters. Late enough that people will have settled down, and with enough time beforehand for me to make coffee without running a military operation.”

“The Taking of Pelham One Two Three,” Owen says. “The original.”

Rosa glances at him. “For the trains.”

“For the pace,” he says. “The trains help.”

Footsteps come down the staircase behind you. A man in a dark work shirt reaches the bottom with his phone to his ear and a small receiver case tucked under one arm.

“No, don’t shift the hotel job for it,” he says into the phone. “It was worth asking. I’ll catch you another time.” He listens a moment, thanks the caller, and ends the call before looking to Nell. “Hana can’t get here before seven.”

“Then we leave the test for another evening,” Nell says. “We’ll look at the diary tomorrow.”

“Fine.” He sets the receiver case carefully beside the office wall. “Dev, by the way.” His attention catches on the conversation at the table. “And mine is Stop Making Sense, if I get the room sounding as it should first.”

“That one at least comes with a reason,” Rosa says.

“So does mine,” Nell says. She takes a stack of bowls from Jo and begins laying them out. “The Towering Inferno.”

Bea looks from Nell to the recently repaired ceiling. “Not during the first month.”

“Not during the first month,” Nell agrees. “A quiet November night, perhaps. When all the fire doors have had time to prove themselves.”

“That’s exactly when you’ll want a film about a building coming apart,” Jo says, carrying the stew through. “You can all have your catastrophe after you’ve eaten something.”

The pot sends up steam scented with cumin and tomatoes as she sets it in the middle of the joined tables. The chairs are no longer quite enough to keep everyone standing around the edges. Jo pulls one back with her knee, then looks across at you.

“You’ve made us sound like a very particular sort of committee, Rowan,” she says. “What would you show first?”
